_note: Three research themes. 'description' paragraphs and 'summary' are edited by hand; 'keywords' decide which papers appear under each theme; 'featured' are the DOIs shown on the research page.

themes.name: Genomic selection and breeding design
themes.summary: How genomic and phenotypic information can be used to predict genetic merit, and how breeding programs can be designed to turn those predictions into sustained genetic gain.
description: Genomic selection has accelerated genetic progress in livestock, but the value of a genomic prediction depends on the information behind it and on the breeding program that acts on it. Our work in this area asks how genomic tools can be used most effectively in practice. It spans the choice of animals to genotype and traits to record, the information included in prediction models, and the design of programs that turn predicted merit into genetic gain without exhausting the genetic variation on which future selection depends.

Much of this work draws on routinely recorded data from commercial and national populations of dairy cattle, beef cattle, and pigs. The statistical methods it relies on are developed in close collaboration with colleagues in statistical genomics at NC State.

themes.name: Inbreeding and genetic diversity
themes.summary: How inbreeding can be measured from genomic data, what it costs in performance, health, and fertility, and how selection can be managed to preserve genetic variation.
description: Selection concentrates genetic contributions on a limited number of families, and genomic selection can accelerate that process. Our work on inbreeding asks how this concentration can be measured, what it costs, and how it can be managed. Genomic data, and runs of homozygosity in particular, describe inbreeding more precisely than pedigrees and separate recent from ancient inbreeding, which can differ in their consequences for production, fertility, health, and longevity.

Estimates of inbreeding depression obtained in this way provide the basis for the mating and selection strategies we evaluate, which aim to sustain genetic gain while curtailing the loss of genetic variation.

themes.name: Host genome, microbiome, and resilience
themes.summary: How the host genome and the gut microbiome jointly shape performance, and how animals respond to heat stress under a changing climate.
description: The performance of an animal, and its capacity to cope with environmental challenges, reflect both its own genome and the microbial communities it carries, and the two are linked because the host genome contributes to shaping those communities. Working mainly in pigs, we examine how host genetics and the gut microbiome jointly influence growth, feed efficiency, and carcass traits, and whether microbial information can improve the prediction of those traits.

The same perspective extends to resilience. Heat stress poses a growing threat to livestock production under climate change. In sows genomically selected for heat tolerance, we combine body temperature records, time-resolved microbiome and other omics data, and genomics to understand how animals respond to heat and how selection can make them more robust.
